name: Anaa-ti
note: Location given as 22° 15′ S, 137° 30′ W, in the Tuamotus. Believed to be a mistaken sighting of a nearby island.

name: Antillia
coord_note: hand-approx: mid-Atlantic as on the 1424 Pizzigano chart
note: The island, like the more popular Atlantis, is a fictional island in the Atlantic originating from an Iberian legend.

name: Antonio d'Ulloa Island
removed_note: 78° 20′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1875.
note: Discovered by the Spanish captain Antonio de Ulloa at 37° 02′ S, 78° 20′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1875.

name: Arthur Island
note: Location given by Arrowsmith as 3° 30′ S, 176° W. Noted to be needing confirmation of existence and position in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Aurora Islands
note: Discovered by Spanish merchant ship Aurora, currently thought to be the Shag Rocks.

name: Bacalao
note: Gaspar Frutuoso noted its discovery by João Vaz Corte-Real in 1472 in Saudades da Terra.

name: Bale of Cotton
removed_note: cally gone onto it. Doubtful by 1817 and not s
coord_note: from notes: 5°22′N and 100 leagues east of Galle
note: A rock in the mouth of the Bay of Bengal, located at 5° 22′ N "100 leagues east from Pointe de Galle." A passenger on the boat that saw the rock claimed to have physically gone onto it. Doubtful by 1817 and not seen on modern maps.

name: Bermeja
note: Discovered in the early 16th century by Spain, but mysteriously vanished sometime during the 17th century. While no dominant theory holds, it is possible that the island submerged due to tectonic movements, supported by the existence of a seamount at and the nearby Scorpion Reef.

name: Bonetta Rocks
removed_note: rde and Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.
note: Location given as 16° 32′ N, 20° 57′ W, between Cape Verde and Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.

name: Bradley Land
note: A mass of land named by Frederick Cook which he claimed to have seen between () and () during a 1909 expedition.

name: Brasil or Hy-Brasil
note: Said to lie in the Atlantic Ocean west of Ireland. Irish myths described it as cloaked in mist except for one day every seven years, when it became visible but still could not be reached. Several 16th century maps showing the island of Brasil also showed an island labelled Demar further south-west.

name: Britomart Island
removed_note: 50' W. Noted to be doubtful in 1851; not seen
note: Discoverer unknown; location given as 19° 52' S, 145° 50' W. Noted to be doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Buss Island
note: Found in the waters near Greenland, in which Martin Frobisher, the leader of the island-finding expedition, probably made a mistake in dead reckoning and mistook optical effects near Greenland for a new island.

name: Cassiterides
note: Ancient source of Phoenician tin. Exact location unknown but thought to have possibly referred to now silt-connected islands within the marshes of Brière.

name: Clark's Reef
note: Discoverer unknown, location given as 8° 18′ S, 139° 50′ (or 52′) W. Admiral Du Petit Thouars could not find the reef, sounding 200 fathoms.

name: Cloate's Island
note: Various locations; sometimes 21° 30′ S, 92° 42′ E, in the Indian Ocean, west of Australia. Probably the headland now known as Point Cloates.

name: Crockerland
note: A hoax invented by Arctic explorer Robert E. Peary to gain more financial aid from George Crocker, one of his financial backers.

name: Davis Land
note: Supposedly sighted by the pirate Edward Davis in the Pacific along the southern latitude of 27 to 28 degrees, which was on the same latitude as the Spanish-controlled gold mines of Copiago. At the time, it was believed that gold could be found elsewhere along the latitude so several navigators were instructed to seek it out on their voyages. Never found, it was also believed by William Dampier to be the coast of Terra Australis Incognita.

name: Isle of Demons
note: Probably a relocated version of the island of Satanazes (see island below).

name: Denia/Davia
note: Location given as 41° or 42° S, 20° E, in close vicinity of Marzeveen/Maarseveen. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Diego Alvarez
note: Location given as 39° 10′ S, 11° 15′ W, between Tristan da Cunha and Gough. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Dougherty Island
note: Because it is near Antarctica, it is likely that the discoverer, Captain Dougherty, and future explorers who confirmed it, saw fog banks and icebergs conveniently situated in the right place and time.

name: Dragon Island
removed_note: , 136° 36′ W. Found nonexistent in 1875.
note: Reported by Capt. Andrew of the bark Dragon at 24° 30′ N, 136° 36′ W. Found nonexistent in 1875.

name: Dunkin's Reef
removed_note: ive shoal. Noted as doubtful and possibly a mistaken sighting in 1851; not seen
note: Discovered by Dunkin; location given as 9° 50′ N, 154° 10′ E. Described as an extensive shoal. Noted as doubtful and possibly a mistaken sighting in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Elizabeth Island
removed_note: s circumnavigation. Not found by subsequent explorers; in 1939 Felix Rie
note: Described by Francis Drake, who reported harbouring there during his circumnavigation. Not found by subsequent explorers; in 1939 Felix Riesenberg suggested Pactolus Bank as a possible remnant, though recent surveys suggest the Bank may itself be a phantom feature.

name: Emerald Island
note: Probably fog banks and icebergs (see Dougherty Island above); the abyssal plain below it was named Emerald Plain, however, in recognition of the nonexistent island.

name: Emily Rock
note: Sighted at 25° 38' S, 87° 25' W by the bark Emily. Reportedly measured to be 15' tall and 120' long. 2 other sightings were reported in 1873, now described as being 3/4th mile long and 20 feet at its tallest point, made of sandy volcanic stone. Several vessels passed through the area but did not see it.

name: Ernest Legouve Reef
note: A reef supposedly found by the captain of the French ship, Ernest Legouvé, which is near the exact location of the fictional Lincoln Island, the main setting for Jules Verne's book The Mysterious Island, also appearing in In Search of the Castaways.

name: Estotiland
note: An island appearing on the Zeno map at the current location of Labrador.

name: Faith Island
note: Location given as 21° 10′ S, 138° 52′ W, in the Tuamotus. Believed to be a mistaken sighting of a nearby island.

name: Fata Morgana Land
note: J.P. Koch, together with Aage Bertelsen, was reported to have first seen Fata Morgana Land () lying in the Arctic Ocean around 80°00´N 10°00´W between NE Greenland and Svalbard. This elusive land was allegedly seen as well by Lauge Koch from the air in 1933.

name: Filippo Reef
note: This reef, part of the Line Islands, was first seen by the ship Filippo and was seen again in 1926 when both ships saw breakers in the same area, suggesting a depth of . Current observations show the reported location to have a depth of , and the nearest shallow seamount is about deep, disproving the existence of the island.

name: Fonseca Island
note: An island sighted east of Barbados.

name: Frisland
note: Another island on the Zeno map, possibly a renamed Iceland.

name: Ganges Island
note: A nonexistent island off the coast of Japan to the southwest of the Shatsky Rise.

name: Haymet Rocks
note: Reported to be located South of Rarotonga; two rocks, about 0.25 miles apart, with 7 or 8 feet of water over them; have not been found since.

name: Humphrey Island
removed_note: ce and was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
note: Discoverer unknown; location given as 16° 52' S, 140° 30' W. Krusenstern doubted its existence and was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Hyperborea
note: Hypothetic land of a mythical people living in the far north of the known world, depicted as the mirror continent of Antarctica on the Mercator map.

name: Ilha de Vera Cruz
coord_note: Porto Seguro Brazil (Brazil mistaken for an island)
note: A supposed 'island' found by Portuguese explorers, which turned out not to be an island but rather what is currently known as Brazil.

name: Jacquet Island
note: An island just to the east of the Flemish Cap; it was believed to exist into the 19th century, during which cartographers discussed it as a possible midway point for the Transatlantic telegraph cable.

name: Jupiter Reef
note: Nonexistent reef in the Line Islands (in fact Line Islands are more than away), to the south of the also nonexistent Ernest Legouve Reef (see above).

name: Keenan Land
coord_note: hand-approx: Beaufort Sea north of Alaska
note: Large landmass reportedly discovered in the Arctic north of Alaska; numerous searches failed to relocate it.

name: Kentzell's Island
removed_note: ru in 1859. Finally disproven by a survey in 1867.
note: Reported by Capt. Kentzell of San Francisco at approx. 40° N, 150° 30′ W. The island, 20 miles long and "very low," was said to have a large seal and sea elephant population, and therefore was kept secret by seal hunters. Searches failed to find it while sightings still came in through the 1860s, including one by the Kanrin Maru in 1859. Finally disproven by a survey in 1867.

name: Kettendyk's Droogte
note: Location given as 33° S, 4° 25′ E, northeast of Tristan da Cunha and west of South Africa. Unsuccessfully searched for, and not seen on modern maps.

name: Krusenstern Rock
note: Reported as a breaker at 22° 15' N, 175° 37' W. Capt. R. Suffern of the Craigerne reported that he was at these exact coordinates in 1897 but there was no sign of the rock.

name: L'Enfants Perdu Islands
removed_note: , 176° 40′ W. Found doubtful in 1875 after sea
note: Discovered by Bougainville, variously placed at 14° 16′ S, 177° 23′ W or 14° 20′ S, 176° 40′ W. Found doubtful in 1875 after searches found no land in the area. Possibly a mistaken sighting of the Horne Islands.

name: Jane Island
removed_note: 10′ N, 173° 15′ W. Could not be found in 1841, and the
note: Location given as 16° 10′ N, 173° 15′ W. Could not be found in 1841, and the island being a mistaken sighting of Johnston Atoll was ruled out due to latitude. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Los Jardines
note: A pair of phantom islands to the east of the Marshall Islands.

name: Jesus Island
removed_note: and it was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
note: Reported by Mendaña at 6° 45′ S, 171° 30′ E. Krusenstern doubted its existence and it was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Maria Theresa Reef (aka Tabor Island or Tabor Reef)
note: Another nonexistent reef in the Line Islands (in fact Line Islands are more than away), slightly to the southwest-west of the phantom island, Jupiter Reef. It is a setting for Jules Verne's book In Search of the Castaways.

name: Maria Rock
removed_note: off of Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.
note: Location given as 19° 45′ N, 20° 50′ W, off of Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.

name: Marzeveen/Maarseveen
note: Location given as 41° or 42° S, 20° E, in close vicinity of Denia/Davia. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Maury Island
note: Location given as 27° S, 95° 06′ W. Not seen on modern maps, but could not be located on any historical maps either.

name: Mayda or Isle of Mam
note: A crescent-shaped island in the North Atlantic that does not appear to exist; however, there is a crescent-shaped group of seamounts deep near its described location.

name: Merrill Island
removed_note: ng Hawaiians. Noted doubtful in 1851; not seen
note: Reported by Captain Harding Merrill of the Comboy at 16° 38′ S, 141° W. Reportedly inhabited by people resembling Hawaiians. Noted doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Islas de Mesa
removed_note: These islands were removed from Spanish charts after James Cook landed in Hawaiʻi in 1778, and it i
note: A Spanish navigator named Juan Gaetano charted an archipelago of islands in the Central Pacific Ocean at approximately 20° N, 138° W that he named the "Islas de Mesa," with islands named , , and . These islands were removed from Spanish charts after James Cook landed in Hawaiʻi in 1778, and it is believed that the "Islas de Mesa" are actually the Hawaiian Islands with their location recorded as being 17 degrees of longitude west of their actual location (an error of about ) due to Gaetano's inability to accurately find their longitude.

name: Minnehaha Rock
note: Sighted by Capt. Beckwith of the Victoria at 25° 50' S, 106° 20' W. No subsequent sightings have been made.

name: Nachtegal Rock
note: Seen by at 40° 20′ S, 52° 55′ E. Last seen in charts in 1878.

name: Nameless Island
removed_note: 70° 18′ E. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
note: Discoverer unknown; location given as 2° 50′ S, 170° 18′ E. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: New Badalgo
note: Location given as 18° 15′ N, 143° 40′ W. Not seen on modern maps.

name: New South Greenland
note: Unknown odd island near Antarctica, which captain Benjamin Morrell of the ship Wasp saw while traveling north from Antarctica. He thought it to be the Antarctic Peninsula (then called New South Greenland), but his reported location during the voyage, while perfectly copying the expected path for traveling up the peninsula, was over to the east and to the north of the actual position of the Antarctic Peninsula, suggesting either a huge miscalculation in location or sightings of icebergs and fog, typical of phantom islands in the Antarctic Circle.

name: New York and Nexsen Islands
note: Reported by a Mr. Fanning on the Betsy at 8° 9′ S, 141° 30.5′ W based on location seven hours after sighting. Smoke noted, suggesting inhabitants. Observed from four to six leagues away and not approached. Suspected in 1851 to be a mistaken sighting of two nearby islands; not seen on modern maps.

name: Nimrod Islands
note: A group of islands between Emerald Island and Dougherty Island, both of which are nonexistent. Probably a group of icebergs together.

name: Pactolus Bank
note: An oceanic bank deep off the west coast of Cape Horn, suggested as the remains of Elizabeth Island. A 1956 search of the area turned up no shallow areas in the reported location.

name: Passion/Paxarus Island
note: Location given as 25° 48′ N, 136° 36′ W or 26° 12′ N, 136° W. No sign of the island could be found in 1873.

name: Pepys Island
note: In 1683, Ambrose Cowley reported an unknown island where he thought the Falklands were, but his location was 4 degrees to the north of the Falkland Islands. While it is possible that he made a mistake in seeing a nonexistent island, it is more likely he saw one of the Falkland Islands and made a 4-degree error in his location.

name: Isle Phelipeaux
removed_note: A nonexistent island in Lake Superior referenced in the 1783 Treaty of
note: A nonexistent island in Lake Superior referenced in the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

name: Podesta
note: An island to the west of El Quisco, Chile, that was discovered to be fake in 1935 and promptly removed. Other phantom islands were also found in the vicinity in 1912 and 1858 (see Sarah Ann Island).

name: Polvaro Island
note: Usually placed at or near 9° 20′ S, 89° E. Reportedly discovered after a Portuguese ship withdrawing from Malacca to Cape Comorin was lost nearby. Sometimes called Apaluria; sighted into the 18th century. Said to be low, woody, eight to 10 miles long. Absence noted in 1866; allegedly "exploded."

name: Recreation Island
removed_note: th no sign of land, removed in 1864.
note: Location given as 15° 35′ S, 150° W, north of Tahiti. Position passed over with no sign of land, removed in 1864.

name: Reed/Redfield Rocks
note: First sighting reported by Capt. Reed of the brig Emma at 37° 24′ N, 137° 22′ W in the Shipping Gazette. More sightings were made in varying locations in 1851, 1856, and 1866. They were said to be two rocks, 600–900 feet long and 50–40 feet across, under 3–5 fathoms of water and breakers in rough weather. Four surveys from 1871 to 1875 could not find them, but another sighting in 1889 said they were now four feet above the water. Another survey in 1902 disproved their existence, but were still marked on maps as doubtful.

name: Rivadeneyra Shoal
note: A shoal in the eastern Pacific Ocean.

name: Ilha dos Romeiros
removed_note: scar and Australia. Removed from charts by 1856 or earlie
note: Location given as 28° 40′ S, 74° E, between Madagascar and Australia. Removed from charts by 1856 or earlier.

name: Roque Piz
note: First seen in a chart by João Teixeora, located at 6° S, 60° E. Seen on maps as late as 1865, described as being three flat islands. Likely a mistaken sighting of the Seychelles or Chagos.

name: Royal Company's Islands
removed_note: of Tasmania. While not found by numerous expeditions in 1840, 1889, 19
note: A fictional island widely believed during the 19th century to be to the southwest of Tasmania. While not found by numerous expeditions in 1840, 1889, 1902, 1909, and 1912, the island was not officially removed from nautical charts until 1904.

name: Rupes Nigra
note: A magnetic, black island at the exact Magnetic North Pole, invented as an explanation for why all compasses point north.

name: Saint Brendan's Island
coord_note: hand-approx: west of the Canary Islands
note: Claimed to have been first visited in 512 by the monk St. Brendan and 14 others, along with later reports up to 1772.

name: St. Elmo
removed_note: umference. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
note: Reported by Quiros, location 21° 20' S, 143° 50' W. Said to be low, surrounded by coral reefs, with a 30 Spanish leagues circumference. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: St. Matthew Island
note: An island near the coast of Africa, roughly east-northeast of Ascension Island and possibly confused with the same latitude Annobón Island.

name: Sandy Island
removed_note: corded on many maps until 2012, when a s
note: Another phantom, small island to the west of New Caledonia that was recorded on many maps until 2012, when a surveying ship passed by and disproved its existence. The current leading explanation is that the island was a raft of buoyant pumice from a recent nearby seamount eruption.

name: Sannikov Land
note: An island near the De Long Islands, north of Russia, that probably did exist but was destroyed due to coastal erosion.

name: Sarah Ann Island
note: A phantom island near Easter Island, similar to Podesta island. See [http://www.lib.utexas.edu/maps/onc/txu-pclmaps-oclc-8322829_r_22.jpg Operational Navigation Chart] of the United States Department of Defense.

name: Satanazes
coord_note: hand-approx: north of Antillia on the 1424 Pizzigano chart
note: This island was originally noted on maps in 1424, originating from popular legend of devils and demons attacking ships that went into the area, but the island was subsequently removed because it obviously did not exist. The island, often drawn to the north of the mythical Antillia, was purportedly full of evil demons but was sometimes called Salvaga to avoid using the profanity "devil".

name: Saxemberg Island
note: An odd island midway between South America and Africa that numerous captains reported seeing in 1804, 1809, and 1816. While most had conflicting reports, all of them found the island in the same location; however, none of them actually made landfall. It is possible the island was volcanic and later erupted and destroyed itself. It is also possible that they were looking at Tristan de Cunha island.

name: Schjetman Reef
note: To the west of the Hawaiian Islands, Schjetman Reef was originally found in 1868 to be an island long and wide. Later searches in 1880, 1923, and 1924 could not find the island.

name: Terra Nova Islands
note: Thought to lie off Oates Coast, East Antarctica.

name: Thompson Island
note: An island in the south Atlantic Ocean discovered by the whaling ship captain George Norris; it has not been seen since 1893.

name: Thule
coord_note: hand-approx: six days' sail north of Britain (Pytheas); article coords were the modern Thule
note: A mythical island in the far north, possibly at or above the Arctic Circle, mentioned in many works from the Roman and Medieval period. Sources in antiquity placed Thule several days travel north of Great Britain visible from Orkney; or north of Scythia. More modern scholars have suggested Thule may have been Ireland; the Estonian island of Saaremaa; or the Norwegian island of Smøla.

name: Tiburones
removed_note: 1° S, 143° W; noted doubtful in 1851 and not s
note: Captain D'Urville asked the residents of Uapoa about this island in August 1838. They claimed it existed, reporting it had high land, one sandy beach which could be approached in good weather, and a single male inhabitant (the others having fled). Location given as 11° S, 143° W; noted doubtful in 1851 and not seen on modern maps.

name: Transit Reef
note: A possible reef in Southern Palau. While this reef probably exists, some maps do not list it as an actual location, and, although the reef doesn't have any land, the native name of the island, Pieraurou, means 'Sandy Navigation Point', implying a sandy island or sand bar.

name: Truls Island
note: Reported by the tanker Truls at 56° S, 23° 15′ E. Marked on USHO Chart 5188B in October 1969 as "ED" (existence doubtful).

name: Turnbull Island
removed_note: 43° 32′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1864 and remov
note: Location given as 19° 52′ S, 143° 32′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1864 and removed from charts after 1875.

name: Two Brothers Reef
removed_note: 8° 28′ W. Existence doubtful by 1912 due to la
note: Reportedly struck by a whaling ship in 1823, location listed as 24° 14' N, 168° 28′ W. Existence doubtful by 1912 due to lack of sightings; not seen on modern maps.

name: Wachusett Reef
note: A nonexistent reef in the Line Islands – in fact Line Islands are more than away – along with Ernest Legouve Reef, Jupiter Reef, and Maria Theresa Reef. This reef, the largest of the three, was thought to be deep. None of these reefs are currently believed to have actually existed.

name: (unnamed bank)
note: Shown on historical charts at 30° 55' N, 177° 30' E and 42 fathoms deep. Soundings of this area in 1901 and 1902 failed to locate the bottom at 100 fathoms, and it is not seen on modern maps.

name: (unnamed rock)
note: Sighted by the steamer Great Pacific at 25° 40' S, 85° 0' W. The Sumbawa passed through the area in 1904 but did not see it.

name: (unnamed breakers)
note: Reported at 21° 55' N, 176° 05' W. There is no indication of these breakers on modern maps.
